title: Event Propagation & Delegation
summary: **Event propagation** is how an event travels through the DOM — down in the **capture** phase, to the **target**, then up in the **bubble** phase. **Event delegation** exploits bubbling by putting a single listener on a parent and using `event.target` (and `closest()`) to handle clicks from many children, including ones added later.

subtopics.title: The three propagation phases
subtopics.explanation: When an event fires, it travels in three phases: CAPTURE (from the document root down toward the target), TARGET (at the element itself), and BUBBLE (back up from the target to the root). By default listeners run in the bubble phase; pass { capture: true } to run during capture. This path is why an event on a child can be observed on its ancestors.
subtopics.example: parent.addEventListener('click', fn, { capture: true }); // runs on the way down

subtopics.title: Bubbling in practice
subtopics.explanation: Most UI events (click, input, keydown) bubble: a click on a button also triggers click listeners on its parents in order from target upward. Some events (focus, blur, mouseenter) do NOT bubble — use their bubbling counterparts (focusin, focusout, mouseover) when you need delegation. Bubbling is what makes delegation possible.
subtopics.example: list.addEventListener('click', (e) => { /* fires for clicks on any child */ });

subtopics.title: event.target vs event.currentTarget
subtopics.explanation: `event.target` is the deepest element where the event originated (the actual thing clicked). `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is currently running (where you called addEventListener). In delegation, currentTarget is the parent and target is the specific child — the distinction is essential to handle the right element.

subtopics.title: stopPropagation()
subtopics.explanation: Calling stopPropagation on the event halts its travel through the remaining phases, so ancestor listeners won't fire. Use it sparingly — it can break delegation and outside-click handlers that rely on bubbling. stopImmediatePropagation additionally prevents other listeners on the SAME element from running.

subtopics.title: The delegation pattern
subtopics.explanation: Instead of attaching a listener to every child, attach ONE listener to a stable parent. Inside it, inspect event.target to decide what was clicked and act accordingly. This works for elements that don't exist yet at setup time, because the listener lives on the parent that persists.

subtopics.title: Matching with closest()
subtopics.explanation: Clicks often land on a nested element (an icon inside a button). element.closest(selector) walks up from event.target to find the nearest matching ancestor (or itself), so you reliably get the logical item even when the user clicked a child of it. Combine with a guard for null when nothing matches.

subtopics.title: Performance & memory benefits
subtopics.explanation: One delegated listener replaces hundreds of per-item listeners: less setup time, lower memory, and automatic support for dynamically added items. For large or frequently changing lists (tables, feeds, todo lists), delegation is the idiomatic, scalable approach — and avoids leaks from forgotten per-item cleanup.
subtopics.example: // one listener on <tbody> handles clicks for thousands of rows

subtopics.title: When NOT to delegate
subtopics.explanation: Delegation isn't free in clarity: deep DOMs and non-bubbling events complicate it, and very specific handlers may be simpler attached directly. For a handful of static elements, direct listeners are clearer. Delegate when items are numerous, dynamic, or share behavior.
subtopics.example: // a single static button: just btn.addEventListener('click', fn)

foundations.overview: Every DOM event flows along a path between the document root and the element that triggered it. Listeners on ancestors can observe events from descendants because the event bubbles up through them. Delegation turns this into a pattern: one parent listener handling many children, identified at runtime via the event's target.
foundations.formalDefinition: Event propagation is the dispatch of an Event along the ancestor chain of its target in three phases (capturing, at-target, bubbling). Event delegation is a design pattern that registers a single listener on a common ancestor and determines the originating element via event.target, typically resolved to a logical element with Element.closest().
foundations.whyItMatters: Delegation is the standard way to handle interactions in lists, tables, menus, and any dynamic content. Understanding propagation also explains otherwise-mysterious bugs where clicks trigger (or fail to trigger) ancestor handlers.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture the event as a ripple: it dives down from the top of the DOM to the clicked element (capture), touches it (target), then ripples back up to the top (bubble). A delegated listener is a net stretched across a parent that catches every ripple coming from its children.
foundations.browserPerspective: On dispatch, the browser computes the event path (the ancestor chain), then walks it twice: down calling capture listeners, then up calling bubble listeners, invoking each registered handler with target fixed and currentTarget set to the node being visited.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Todo lists with delete buttons, data tables with row actions, dropdown menus, tag inputs, and infinite-scroll feeds all use one delegated listener on the container rather than per-item listeners.
foundations.businessImpact: Delegation keeps large, dynamic interfaces fast and memory-light, which protects engagement on data-heavy pages; misusing stopPropagation, however, can silently break features like 'click outside to close'.
foundations.engineeringImpact: It reduces boilerplate and eliminates per-item cleanup, but requires fluency with target vs currentTarget and closest() to route events correctly.
foundations.performanceImpact: Replacing N listeners with 1 cuts setup time and memory dramatically and removes a class of leaks; the tiny per-event cost of matching the target is negligible.
commonUseCases: Handling actions for dynamically added list/table rows
Routing clicks in menus and toolbars from one container listener
Reducing memory in large lists by avoiding per-item listeners

commonMisconceptions.myth: event.target is the element you attached the listener to.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That's currentTarget; target is the deepest element where the event actually originated.

commonMisconceptions.myth: stopPropagation also cancels the default action.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It only stops travel through the DOM; canceling default behavior needs preventDefault.

commonMisconceptions.myth: All events bubble, so delegation always works.
commonMisconceptions.reality: focus, blur, and mouseenter don't bubble — use focusin/focusout/mouseover for delegation.

debuggingLab.title: Delete buttons don't work on newly added rows
debuggingLab.symptom: Clicking 'x' deletes the original rows but does nothing for rows added after the page loaded.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: querySelectorAll runs once at load and binds listeners only to the buttons present then. Rows added later get fresh '.del' buttons that were never bound, so clicking them does nothing. Per-item binding can't cover future elements.
commonMistakes: Querying and binding once instead of delegating to a stable parent.
Re-running the query after each insert (works but is wasteful and leak-prone).
Assuming a class selector keeps matching new elements automatically.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make delete work for every row — current and future — using a single listener.

theory.question: Explain the three phases of event propagation.
theory.directAnswer: When an event is dispatched it travels through three phases: capturing (from the document root down to the target's parent), at-target (on the element itself), and bubbling (back up from the target to the root). Listeners run in the bubble phase by default; { capture: true } makes them run during the capture phase instead.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The defined path and order in which an event visits the target's ancestors.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It lets ancestors observe or intercept descendant events, enabling patterns like delegation and outside-click detection.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser computes the ancestor chain, walks down invoking capture listeners, fires at-target listeners, then walks up invoking bubble listeners.

theory.whyImportant: It explains why a click on a child can trigger parent handlers and underpins delegation, the standard pattern for dynamic UIs.
theory.realWorldExample: A document-level click listener closes a dropdown when you click anywhere outside it, relying on bubbling.

nestedTopics.title: Capture vs bubble
nestedTopics.explanation: Down then up; default listeners are bubble-phase.

followUps.question: How do you make a listener run during capture?
followUps.answer: Pass { capture: true } (or true as the third argument) to addEventListener.

theory.question: What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
theory.directAnswer: event.target is the deepest element where the event originated — the actual element the user interacted with. event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently executing, i.e. the one you called addEventListener on. In delegation, target is the specific child and currentTarget is the parent holding the listener.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two Event properties identifying the origin element versus the listening element.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Delegation requires knowing both where the event started and where you're handling it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: target is fixed for the whole dispatch; currentTarget changes to each node as the event propagates through it.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing them is a top source of delegation bugs (acting on the wrong element).
theory.realWorldExample: In a list listener, currentTarget is the <ul> while target is the clicked <button> inside an <li>.

nestedTopics.title: closest()
nestedTopics.explanation: Resolves target up to the logical item, e.g. the <li>.

nestedTopics.title: matches()
nestedTopics.explanation: Tests whether target matches a selector to filter clicks.

followUps.question: Why use closest() instead of target directly?
followUps.answer: Users may click a nested element (an icon inside a button); closest walks up to the real interactive item.

scenario.question: A data table with thousands of rows is slow to render and uses a lot of memory because each row has several click listeners. How would you improve it?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd replace per-row/per-button listeners with event delegation: a single listener on the table body. Inside it I'd use event.target.closest() to find the clicked action and the owning row (via a data attribute or row index), then dispatch the right handler. This cuts setup time, slashes memory, removes per-row cleanup, and automatically covers rows added by pagination or virtualization.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Refactoring many listeners into one delegated listener on a stable ancestor.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Per-item listeners scale poorly in count and memory; bubbling lets one listener serve all items.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The single listener inspects target/closest to route each event to the correct logical element.

scenario.whyImportant: It directly improves performance and memory on data-heavy pages and simplifies dynamic content handling.

nestedTopics.title: data-* attributes
nestedTopics.explanation: Encode row id/action on elements for the delegated handler to read.

nestedTopics.title: Virtualization
nestedTopics.explanation: Delegation pairs naturally with windowed lists where rows mount/unmount.

followUps.question: What are the downsides of delegation here?
followUps.answer: Slightly more complex routing logic, reliance on bubbling, and care needed if a child calls stopPropagation or for non-bubbling events.

coding.question: Write delegate(parent, selector, type, handler) that calls handler only when the event's target matches selector, with `this`/the resolved element passed in.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll attach one listener to the parent. On each event I use target.closest(selector) to find the matching element, verify it's inside the parent, and if found call the handler with that element. This is the core of jQuery-style delegated events and supports dynamic children automatically.
coding.lineByLine: One listener on `parent` handles all matching descendants. `closest(selector)` resolves the originating node up to the intended element; `parent.contains(match)` guards against matches outside the container; `handler.call(match, e, match)` invokes the callback with the resolved element as both `this` and an argument.
coding.timeComplexity: O(d) per event where d is DOM depth from target to match (closest walk); effectively constant.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a single listener regardless of child count.

alternativeApproaches.title: matches() instead of closest()
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If you only handle direct clicks on the element (no nested children), test e.target.matches(selector).

followUps.question: Why check parent.contains(match)?
followUps.answer: closest can match an ancestor outside the parent; the guard ensures the matched element is actually within the delegated container.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Delegation centralizes interaction handling on container components, which fits component models and virtualized lists where children constantly mount and unmount. It also mirrors how frameworks like React implement their synthetic event system at the root.
productionDeepDive.performance: One listener instead of thousands reduces memory and registration cost and avoids re-binding on every list change; the per-event closest() walk is negligible compared to per-item listener overhead.
productionDeepDive.security: When routing on data attributes, treat their values as untrusted input; never inject them into innerHTML. Be wary of stopPropagation breaking security-relevant outside-click handlers (e.g., closing sensitive menus).
productionDeepDive.scaling: Delegation is the default for large tables, feeds, and trees; it scales to arbitrarily many items because cost is independent of item count.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: A single, well-documented delegated handler with clear selector routing is easier to reason about than scattered per-item bindings, though deep selector logic should be factored into small functions.
productionDeepDive.observability: DevTools 'Event Listeners' shows the single parent listener; if clicks aren't handled, inspect whether a child called stopPropagation or whether the event bubbles at all.

caseStudies.problem: Attaching listeners to every node was expensive and complex with dynamic trees.
caseStudies.solution: A root-level delegated synthetic event system that routes events to the right component.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: An abstraction and reliance on bubbling vs. far lower listener count and consistent cross-browser behavior.
caseStudies.lessons: Delegation at a stable root is the scalable foundation for dynamic UIs.

keyTakeaways: Events propagate in three phases: capture (down), target, then bubble (up); listeners default to the bubble phase.
event.target is where the event originated; event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running.
Delegation attaches ONE listener to a stable parent and routes events via event.target, automatically covering dynamic children.
Use closest(selector) to resolve a clicked nested element up to its logical item; use matches() to filter targets.
Delegation cuts memory and setup cost dramatically for large/dynamic lists; use stopPropagation sparingly so you don't break delegation or outside-click handlers.
